transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Route-level A/B testing framework - kickoff
Date: 2026-02-03
Time: 09:00–09:56 PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Marissa Cole (Product)
- Dylan Brooks (Eng, Console & Tooling)
- Jada Williams (Backend architect, A/B framework)
- Ethan Park (Control-plane)
- Mina Haddad (Routing)
- Logan Wright (Telemetry/Analytics)
- Nadia Rahman (Cost attribution & metering)
- Sean Gallagher (SRE)
- Tessa Morgan (Design)
- Jonas Weber (Applied ML/Evals)
- Talia Benson (Program Mgmt)

---
Auto Summary (generated)
- Team aligned on initial scope: route-level A/B experiments configured in Console with deterministic assignment, exposure logging, and v1 reporting on latency/cost/errors.
- Key risks highlighted: metric cardinality blowups, assignment stickiness across retries/streaming, and precedence interactions with canary/fallback policies.
- Agreed on phased delivery (backend primitives → Console CRUD → reporting + guardrails → eval attachments → hardening/GA).
- Action items assigned for assignment semantics, event schema, guardrails, and initial Console flow.

Topics
1) What problem we’re solving / v1 scope
2) Routing + assignment model
3) Telemetry: exposure logs, metrics, cost attribution
4) Console workflows and terminology
5) Guardrails, SLOs, rollback, audit
6) Quality/evals integration (v1 vs later)
7) Timeline and owners

Action Items (quick list)
- Jada to draft deterministic assignment semantics
- Logan/Nadia to draft exposure + metrics schema with strict cardinality rules
- Sean to propose guardrail thresholds and alert routing
- Tessa to share first UX flow + copy/terminology options
- Mina to confirm precedence with canary/fallback

Questions (captured)
- What is the canonical “sticky key” when user_id is missing? api_key_id? tenant_id? custom header?
- Do we support more than 2 variants in v1 or hard limit to A/B?
- Where do we emit exposure events: gateway only, or also in runtime for retries?
- How do we avoid high-cardinality tags when customers name variants/experiments freely?
- When an experiment is paused/stopped, do we continue logging exposures for in-flight streams?

---
Transcript

[00:00] Marissa Cole: Okay, cool, looks like folks are joining. I’ll give it like thirty seconds.

[00:18] Marissa Cole: Alright. Thanks everyone. This is the kickoff for route-level A/B testing in Console. The goal today is to align on scope, roles, timeline, and the big scary risks so we don’t step on a rake later.

[00:34] Dylan Brooks: And to be explicit, this is the Console-first workflow, but there’s a bunch of routing and telemetry underneath. So we just want to get ahead of dependencies.

[00:44] Talia Benson: I’ll take notes and I’ll also capture owners for action items as we go.

[00:49] Marissa Cole: Great. Quick framing. We already have canaries and model pinning and fallback routing. Customers keep asking, “Can I split traffic for my /v1/chat route between two model configs and see latency and cost and errors side by side?” That’s the core.

[01:08] Marissa Cole: v1: create an experiment on a route, choose variants (model version + config), pick split like 90/10 or 50/50, start/stop, and see results. And we need it to be safe—guardrails, rollback, audit logs.

[01:27] Sean Gallagher: From SRE side, “safe” means we can auto page or auto rollback if someone accidentally routes 50% into a tiny pool and we get 429s.

[01:35] Marissa Cole: Yep, exactly.

[01:40] Jada Williams: And “deterministic” means if the same user comes back, they should consistently see variant A or B, not flip on every request.

[01:48] Marissa Cole: Right. So let’s go around quickly—roles and what you’re responsible for. Dylan?

[01:56] Dylan Brooks: I’m leading the Console and tooling side. Chloe couldn’t make it, but she’ll own backend CRUD APIs for the Console service. I’ll coordinate the UI pieces with Tessa.

[02:08] Jada Williams: I’ll own overall framework backend architecture—assignment library, policy model, and how it plugs into routing.

[02:16] Ethan Park: Control-plane side. Config storage, policy evaluation service, and ensuring this works in Hosted and Dedicated. Private maybe later.

[02:24] Mina Haddad: Routing lead. I’ll handle precedence with existing rollout policies and how gateway picks an upstream.

[02:31] Logan Wright: Telemetry and analytics. Exposure events schema, ingestion, aggregation for the dashboard.

[02:37] Nadia Rahman: Cost attribution and metering. Making sure experiment + variant dims show up consistently in token cost and GPU attribution.

[02:44] Sean Gallagher: Operational readiness—guardrails, alerts, runbooks, and what we require before beta enablement.

[02:51] Tessa Morgan: Design lead for Console flows. Kenji will help on IA/copy, he’s heads down this morning.

[02:59] Jonas Weber: Evals integration. v1 offline suite attachment and quality deltas, but I want to be careful about how we show stats so we don’t imply meaning with tiny N.

[03:09] Marissa Cole: Perfect.

[03:12] Marissa Cole: Now, scope. There’s been some “do we do full experiment platform like Statsig/Optimizely” conversations. We’re not doing that. We’re doing standardized metrics for inference—latency, time to first token, total tokens, error/timeout/429, and cost.

[03:29] Dylan Brooks: And the “route level” is important: not per prompt, not per customer segment beyond eligibility rules, but per API route within a project.

[03:39] Mina Haddad: One nuance: “route” in our system is like a combination of endpoint + project + maybe model group? We need to define the key so we don’t get surprised.

[03:50] Marissa Cole: Yeah, we’ll define “route” as the API endpoint path plus project, and optionally filters like region or tenant. We’ll make it explicit in the PRD.

[04:02] Tessa Morgan: On UI we can keep it customer mental model: “Choose endpoint” and “choose project,” then advanced filters.

[04:10] Logan Wright: From telemetry perspective, we have to avoid too many dimensions. If “route” includes arbitrary headers, we’re in trouble.

[04:18] Marissa Cole: Okay, let’s jump to the biggest risks. Logan, do you want to tee up cardinality?

[04:25] Logan Wright: Sure. If we tag every metric with experiment_id, variant_name, route, project, region, model, customer… you can blow up dashboards and storage.

[04:36] Logan Wright: We need a strict allowlist: experiment_id as a stable ID (not customer-provided string), variant_id (A/B numeric or short), maybe project_id, maybe region, and that’s it. Then anything else must be derived in a lower-cardinality dataset, not timeseries tags.

[04:54] Nadia Rahman: Also for cost attribution, we already dimension by model, org, project. Adding experiment_id+variant_id is okay but we can’t add “prompt_template_name” or whatever.

[05:06] Sean Gallagher: And sampling. Exposure events at full volume might be huge for high throughput customers.

[05:12] Logan Wright: Exactly. So we probably do 100% for aggregate counters/histograms, but exposure logs might be sampled, and we need to separate those two in the doc so people don’t think exposure logs are complete truth.

[05:27] Marissa Cole: Great. Jada, determinism risk?

[05:31] Jada Williams: Yeah. Deterministic assignment is easy if you have a stable key. But we don’t always. In many calls, customers don’t pass user_id.

[05:43] Jada Williams: So what do we hash on? Options: tenant_id (org/project), api_key_id, a customer-provided header like “x-end-user-id.” If you hash on org only you get split by org but not sticky per end user.

[05:58] Dylan Brooks: But customers still want stable per “conversation” sometimes.

[06:02] Jada Williams: Right, for chat you can use conversation_id if they pass it. We should specify a precedence order of keys: explicit experiment_key header first, then user_id header, then api_key_id as fallback.

[06:16] Mina Haddad: And what about retries? If gateway retries, we need to ensure it doesn’t re-bucket.

[06:22] Jada Williams: Exactly. For retries we can include request_id in a way that is stable. But request_id changes across retries sometimes. Another approach is: once gateway picks variant, it sets a header like x-redwood-experiment-variant and passes it along for internal retries.

[06:39] Ethan Park: That’s doable but needs careful threat model. Customers shouldn’t be able to spoof that header and force routing.

[06:46] Mina Haddad: So it has to be internal-only or signed.

[06:49] Sean Gallagher: Also streaming reconnect. Some clients drop stream and reconnect. They’ll send a new request_id. If they don’t include a sticky key, they might flip variants and then your metrics are nonsense.

[07:02] Marissa Cole: Okay, so we need documented semantics. And probably a Console warning: “To ensure stickiness, set header X.”

[07:10] Tessa Morgan: Yeah we can add a validation step in UI: “We detect you’re not sending x-end-user-id; results may vary.” But we might not actually detect it at config time.

[07:21] Dylan Brooks: We can detect at runtime and show “stickiness health” maybe later. For v1 maybe just docs + best practice.

[07:29] Marissa Cole: Let’s park that as an action item: Jada to propose canonical key order and how we handle streaming/retries. Mina, you’ll partner on the routing header/signed header thing.

[07:42] Talia Benson: Captured.

[07:44] Marissa Cole: Next: precedence with canaries/fallback. Mina?

[07:49] Mina Haddad: Today routing has a precedence chain: pinned model, then canary policy, then fallback if upstream errors/capacity.

[07:59] Mina Haddad: With experiments we’re adding another policy. We need to decide if experiment selection happens before canary or after. My instinct: experiment is a routing decision like canary. But fallback should still override if a variant is unhealthy.

[08:14] Dylan Brooks: Console-wise, customers will assume the experiment is the thing controlling split, not a canary silently overriding.

[08:21] Ethan Park: But internally we might have safety canaries we don’t want experiments to break.

[08:26] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. Guardrails should cause rollback or override of variant, which is essentially a fallback.

[08:33] Jada Williams: I propose a clear precedence: first check hard safety overrides (global kill switches, region disable), then apply experiment assignment if enabled, then within each variant apply canary sub-policy? That gets complicated.

[08:49] Mina Haddad: Or simpler: experiment chooses between two “targets,” and each target can itself be a rollout target that may have a canary. But that’s like nesting.

[08:59] Marissa Cole: We need a simple v1 story. Customers aren’t going to understand nested rollouts.

[09:06] Mina Haddad: For v1: disallow overlapping rollouts on same route. If there’s an active canary on the route, you can’t start an experiment until it ends. And vice versa.

[09:18] Tessa Morgan: That’s easier to explain and design, plus UI can warn and block.

[09:24] Sean Gallagher: That’s also safer for us.

[09:27] Marissa Cole: Great. That’s a v1 constraint: no overlapping experiments/canaries for the same route+project. We can revisit later.

[09:36] Dylan Brooks: We’ll need a validator API to check conflicts.

[09:40] Ethan Park: Control-plane can check for overlapping policy objects.

[09:44] Marissa Cole: Cool.

[09:46] Marissa Cole: Telemetry and reporting. Logan, what’s v1 reporting view?

[09:52] Logan Wright: At minimum: exposures over time by variant, p50/p95/p99 latency, TTFT, error rate, 429/timeout, token in/out, cost per request and per 1k tokens. And ability to filter by region and time range.

[10:11] Logan Wright: We need “exposure logging” as an event: when a request is assigned to experiment X variant Y, log it once at gateway.

[10:22] Nadia Rahman: Cost attribution needs to be joined with exposure. Ideally we tag cost events with experiment_id and variant_id at the source so we don’t do huge joins later.

[10:33] Logan Wright: Agree. But we must keep tags limited. experiment_id and variant_id only.

[10:40] Jonas Weber: Also, quality metrics: offline eval suite results aren’t per-request. They’re per run of a prompt set. That’s a different dataset.

[10:49] Marissa Cole: Right. For v1 we’ll treat quality as optional attachment: run eval suite against both variants, show a delta and a confidence range, with big disclaimers.

[11:02] Jonas Weber: And ideally show sample size and “not enough data” states. If N < 100 prompts, don’t show fancy conclusions.

[11:12] Tessa Morgan: We can design the results panel with “Performance” and “Quality” tabs and show “Beta” label.

[11:18] Dylan Brooks: But only if we have the ingestion and API contract.

[11:21] Jonas Weber: I’ll draft what we can safely show.

[11:25] Marissa Cole: Okay.

[11:26] Marissa Cole: Guardrails. Sean, can you outline beta requirements?

[11:31] Sean Gallagher: Yeah. Before we let external customers run this, we need: (1) hard limit on max traffic shift per minute or a safe ramp, (2) alerting keyed by experiment_id, (3) rollback workflow and “emergency disable,” and (4) runbook.

[11:49] Sean Gallagher: Guardrails: if p95 latency regresses > say 15% for 10 minutes or error rate goes above a threshold, we should page and ideally auto rollback to control.

[12:03] Logan Wright: That implies we need near-real-time aggregation.

[12:07] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Doesn’t have to be perfect stats, but enough to catch explosions. Especially 429s.

[12:14] Mina Haddad: 429s might be capacity-driven. If variant B points to a smaller pool, we want to stop sending it more.

[12:22] Marissa Cole: Agreed. We’ll put a default guardrail for 429 and 5xx.

[12:28] Sean Gallagher: Also, audit logs. Any start/stop/rollback must be in audit trail with who did it and from where.

[12:35] Ethan Park: Control-plane can emit audit events on config changes. Console should also show history.

[12:42] Dylan Brooks: We’ll need a “history” tab in UI eventually. v1 maybe basic.

[12:48] Marissa Cole: Okay.

[12:50] Marissa Cole: Timeline. I’m proposing phases: Phase 0: PRD + design spec + ADRs, ~2-3 weeks. Phase 1: backend primitives + telemetry schema + basic Console CRUD, ~4-6 weeks. Phase 2: results UI + guardrails + eval attachment, ~3-5 weeks. Phase 3: hardening + docs + GA checklist.

[13:15] Talia Benson: I’ll turn that into a calendar and a weekly sync.

[13:18] Dylan Brooks: Engineering-wise, biggest long pole is telemetry pipeline changes. So we should start that early.

[13:26] Logan Wright: Yep, the schema and ingestion are critical path.

[13:30] Marissa Cole: Let’s walk through decisions we need ASAP.

[13:34] Marissa Cole: Decision 1: assignment key and stickiness. Jada, can you draft a 1-pager by end of week?

[13:41] Jada Williams: Yes. I’ll include options and a recommended order. Probably “x-redwood-experiment-key” (customer set) -> “x-end-user-id” -> api_key_id -> request_id only for non-sticky mode. And I’ll call out the privacy implications.

[13:57] Ethan Park: Make sure we also cover hashing details and bucket count. Like 10k buckets so we can do 1% splits.

[14:03] Jada Williams: Yep.

[14:05] Marissa Cole: Decision 2: schema and cardinality. Logan and Nadia, can you draft a v1 schema with strict rules?

[14:12] Logan Wright: Yes.

[14:13] Nadia Rahman: Yes, and I’ll include what we can join in billing reports later.

[14:18] Marissa Cole: Decision 3: precedence/conflicts. Mina, you proposed “no overlap with canaries.” Can you confirm with routing and platform?

[14:27] Mina Haddad: Yes. I’ll sanity check with Ravi too and write it down.

[14:31] Marissa Cole: Decision 4: guardrails/alerts. Sean, can you propose thresholds and who gets paged?

[14:39] Sean Gallagher: Yes. I’ll coordinate with Allison for dashboards/alerts patterns.

[14:43] Marissa Cole: Decision 5: Console flows. Tessa, can we get initial wireframes? Especially create → validate → start, and rollback.

[14:52] Tessa Morgan: Yes, I’ll share a first pass. One thing: terminology. Customers got confused with “control” vs “variant A.” We should pick one and be consistent.

[15:03] Dylan Brooks: I prefer “Variant A (Control)” and “Variant B (Challenger)” in UI, but maybe too finance-y.

[15:10] Marissa Cole: Let’s test it with internal dogfood. Also we need to keep it generic for >2 variants later.

[15:17] Jonas Weber: And for evals, “baseline” and “candidate” maps better.

[15:20] Tessa Morgan: I’ll include options.

[15:23] Marissa Cole: Great.

[15:25] (cross talk)

[15:27] Dylan Brooks: One more on validation: We should validate that both variants support the same tool-calling / structured output settings, otherwise results are apples and oranges.

[15:37] Ethan Park: Control-plane can check compatibility: same endpoint type, same streaming mode, etc.

[15:44] Marissa Cole: Good point. That’s part of “validate config.”

[15:48] Logan Wright: Also, metrics comparability: if variant B has different max_tokens or temperature, latency changes might be expected. We should display those config diffs.

[15:59] Tessa Morgan: We can show a “diff” view before starting.

[16:03] Dylan Brooks: Nice.

[16:05] Marissa Cole: Okay, let’s talk briefly about Private and Dedicated support. Ethan?

[16:12] Ethan Park: Hosted and Dedicated should be in-scope for beta. Private maybe gated because telemetry pipeline and Console connectivity is different. We can design the control-plane objects to be compatible, but we might not promise it.

[16:27] Sean Gallagher: For Dedicated, we need to ensure experiment routing doesn’t break their isolation. But since it’s within their dedicated pool, it’s fine.

[16:35] Mina Haddad: Routing layer can respect “pool constraints” per variant.

[16:39] Marissa Cole: We’ll say “Hosted + Dedicated in beta; Private later.”

[16:45] Jonas Weber: For eval suites in Private, it’s tricky anyway because you need to run eval harness where the data is.

[16:51] Marissa Cole: Yep.

[16:52] Marissa Cole: Quick dive on exposure events privacy. Logan?

[16:56] Logan Wright: We should not log raw prompts, obviously. Exposure event should include: timestamp, experiment_id, variant_id, project_id, route_id (internal), region, request_id (maybe hashed), and a stickiness key hash (not the actual user_id).

[17:14] Logan Wright: We need to be careful: if we include api_key_id that might be sensitive but it’s already in internal logs. For experiment reporting, we probably don’t need it.

[17:24] Nadia Rahman: For billing, we already track api_key_id sometimes. But for experiment metrics, I agree, don’t include it.

[17:31] Ethan Park: And we must enforce that customers can’t pass arbitrary strings that become tags. So experiment_id must be generated server-side.

[17:40] Dylan Brooks: UI can allow “name” but we store “id” and we only use id in telemetry.

[17:46] Marissa Cole: Great.

[17:48] Sean Gallagher: Also retention. Exposure logs shouldn’t live forever. Maybe 30 days by default.

[17:55] Logan Wright: We can do retention in the event store and keep aggregated metrics longer.

[18:00] Marissa Cole: Sounds good.

[18:02] (pause)

[18:03] Marissa Cole: Let’s open it up: any concerns not covered?

[18:07] Dylan Brooks: One risk is “experiment results mismatch” — customers compare our dashboard to their own and they don’t line up because of sampling or definitions (TTFT measured where?). We should define metrics precisely.

[18:21] Logan Wright: Yes. We need a metrics definition doc: end-to-end latency vs model latency, TTFT from gateway, token counts from runtime.

[18:30] Sean Gallagher: And we should use the same definitions as existing latency dashboards, otherwise Support gets hammered.

[18:37] Marissa Cole: Okay, add as part of metrics schema doc.

[18:40] Jonas Weber: For quality stats: please no p-values sprinkled around without explanation. Maybe just “difference” and “confidence interval” with a tooltip.

[18:50] Tessa Morgan: We can do “Likely better / unclear / likely worse” but that’s dangerously simplified.

[18:56] Jonas Weber: Exactly. We can do “insufficient evidence” state.

[19:00] Marissa Cole: v1: show the raw numbers + CI and disclaimers.

[19:05] Mina Haddad: Another operational risk: if someone sets 50/50 and one variant is in us-east only, then half the requests from eu-west get cross-region latency.

[19:16] Ethan Park: Eligibility rules should include region constraints.

[19:19] Mina Haddad: We should validate that both variants are available in selected regions.

[19:24] Dylan Brooks: UI validation can show “Variant B not available in eu-west.”

[19:29] Marissa Cole: Great catch. Put in validation.

[19:32] Talia Benson: Noted.

[19:34] Marissa Cole: Okay, I’m going to fast-forward to recap and next steps.

[19:39] Marissa Cole: Recap: We’re building route-level A/B testing in Console. v1 includes deterministic assignment, exposure logging, dashboards for latency/cost/errors, optional offline eval suite attachment, and guardrails with rollback.

[19:54] Marissa Cole: Major constraints for v1: No overlapping canaries/experiments on same route; limited dimensions for metrics to avoid cardinality; assignment key precedence documented; Private likely not in beta.

[20:08] Marissa Cole: Owners: Dylan for Console + backend APIs, Jada for assignment framework, Ethan for control-plane/config, Mina for routing/precedence, Logan/Nadia for telemetry+cost, Sean for guardrails/SRE readiness, Tessa for UX, Jonas for eval integration.

[20:25] Marissa Cole: Action items: Jada deterministic assignment 1-pager, Logan/Nadia schema + sampling, Sean guardrails thresholds, Tessa wireframes/copy, Mina precedence + region availability validation notes, Jonas eval scope.

[20:43] Dylan Brooks: Also, can we agree to a weekly 30-minute sync? Otherwise we’re going to drift.

[20:48] Talia Benson: Yep. I’ll send an invite. Probably Thursdays.

[20:52] Sean Gallagher: Please include SRE in that. We tend to get pulled in late and then we block launches.

[20:57] Marissa Cole: Yep, you’re on it.

[21:00] Marissa Cole: Okay, anything else urgent?

[21:03] (silence)

[21:05] Marissa Cole: Cool. Thanks everyone.

[21:08] (Meeting continues with informal side discussion; recording captured until end)

[21:12] Dylan Brooks: One more quick thing—naming. “Experiment” vs “Test.”

[21:16] Tessa Morgan: I’ll include it in copy. “Experiment” is standard but some customers get nervous.

[21:21] Marissa Cole: We can call it “Traffic split test” in UI and “experiment” in docs. We’ll see.

[21:28] Logan Wright: As long as the ID is experiment_id internally.

[21:31] Sean Gallagher: And a big warning banner when you’re about to start: “This changes production traffic.”

[21:36] Dylan Brooks: Yes.

[21:38] Marissa Cole: Alright, done. Thanks.

[21:41] (crosstalk, meeting ends)
